World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Good behaviour bond given to NDIS worker for fraudulent claims to keep provider afloat
World.content:
An Adelaide man who defrauded the NDIS out of more than $58,000 has been spared jail for the offending, which happened "out of desperation" to keep the struggling business afloat, a court has heard.

Adrian Cameron Bembrick, 41, appeared in Adelaide's District Court for sentencing on Monday.

The court heard he had been working long hours and paying himself less as he tried to manage the wages and outgoings of NDIS provider, People Come First, between July 2019 and March 2020.

In sentencing, Judge Anthony Allen said he had considered that Bembrick's actions were "not for personal gain".

"It was submitted, and I accept that you, during the relevant time were paying yourself less, in fact significantly less, than the salary to which you were entitled," he said.

" Your offending was borne out of desperation to simply keep the organisation afloat in very difficult financial times. "

The court heard Bembrick had pleaded guilty to making a series of dishonest claims to the NDIS. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Bembrick previously pleaded guilty to a charge of obtaining financial advantage by deception for making a series of dishonest claims.

"This offending has completely destroyed your life," Judge Allen said.

"You are a person who has lived an otherwise blameless life, who now finds yourself in a homeless shelter and penniless, alone in a city away from your family.

"Effectively, you've lost everything."

Judge Allen noted a series of references which "speak highly" of Bembrick and stated that the "offending is completely out of character".

"You have undertaken volunteer work in the homeless shelter where you reside and the staff of that organisation also speak highly of you," he said.

Judge Anthony Allen said Adrian Bembrick's offending was out of character. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Judge Allen fixed a sentence of just under one year and eight months in prison, but released Bembrick immediately on a good behaviour bond.

"Whilst general deterrence looms large in matters such as this, circumstances of your offending, in that you were attempting to keep your organisation afloat effectively for the benefit of others, and your personal circumstances, together with the adverse consequences of your actions, which you have already suffered, you'll be released on a recognisance in the amount of $500, requiring that you be of good behaviour for a period of two years," Judge Allen said.

The former Chief Executive Officer of PCF, Paul Kevan Tilbury was jailed in 2025 for defrauding the NDIS of more than $400,000.

Judge Allen noted significant differences between Bembrick's offending and that of Tilbury's in that the latter was making false claims to support "a lifestyle which he otherwise he could not afford".

Bembrick did not comment as he left the District Court building on Monday.

World.title: Social housing demand jumps 500pc in city where baby died in riverside camp
World.content:
A week after a newborn baby died in a riverside camp in Wagga Wagga, a new report has revealed the southern New South Wales city has the state's fastest-growing waitlist for social housing.

The report, by advocacy group Homeless NSW, shows that the number of households on a priority list for social housing more than doubled across the state in the four years to June 2025, with Wagga recording a 500 per cent increase.

Chief executive Dom Rowe said the damning figures coincided with a 48 per cent increase in apartment rents across NSW.

"That's leading to some problematic situations for people looking for shelter, and we can see that in the increase in the priority waitlist," she said.

Dom Rowe says the sharp increase in demand for social housing coincides with the rising rental price for apartments. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

The report shows waitlists growing in both metropolitan and regional areas.

In western Sydney, Camden saw a 494 per cent increase in demand over four years, and there was a 405 per cent jump in Bankstown.

In the regions, Griffith in the state's south-west saw a 450 per cent increase, while in the north, there was a 330 per cent increase in Tamworth.

Emergency plan for Wagga

Wagga became the centre of a national outcry last week after a baby died during birth at a camp where people are living on the banks of the Murrumbidgee River.

Some residents living in the camp told the ABC that while temporary accommodation was available, it was not suitable for them.

Following a meeting led by NSW Premier Chris Minns on Friday, a cross-agency group made up of representatives from Homes NSW, NSW Police and the Wagga Wagga City Council was set up to prioritise getting rough sleepers into more permanent forms of housing.

"I'm assured that the resources are there, and those options around accommodation are there," independent Wagga Wagga MP Joe McGirr said.

"I specifically sought assurances in that regard."

Joe McGirr says he has been assured people will be offerred appropriate accommodation. (ABC News: Lauren Pezet)

Dr McGirr was unable to explain the kind of accommodation that would be made available, but when pushed about what would be different from what those people had previously been offered, said it was "about being more assertive in the outreach".

"Sometimes people are anxious about the options," he said.

"They're worried about cost, for example, and the long-term situation.

" But it's not appropriate for people to continue to live in those circumstances, and we need to support people to find alternatives. "

Ms Rowe said technology such as modular construction meant appropriate housing could be built "in a matter of days".

"It's created in a factory and can be put up very quickly on site," she said.

"The houses are very, very amenable. They look very good, and they are very safe for people."

Modular social housing Residents have moved in to the largest modular social housing development in New South Wales.

In terms of land, she said there were two options readily available that already had access to services such as running water.

"One of those is government land," Ms Rowe said.

"That's all around New South Wales and often is very well located to amenities.

" The other thing that people are exploring at the moment is faith-based land … churches and places of worship where there's serious amounts of grounds around those places of worship, which could fit a number of houses on those areas. "

Wagga could become state model

Wagga's mayor, Dallas Tout, said he had been speaking to other mayors around the state about how they were dealing with similar issues.

Cr Tout said he hoped Wagga could set an example.

"I would imagine as this stands up and this works through, they will also be looking at other areas as well," he said.

"It's something you could, template is probably an inappropriate word, but it's something you could take with this approach."

The NSW Minister for Homelessness, Rose Jackson, is expected to visit Wagga in the coming weeks and was contacted for comment.

World.title: Indulgent breakfast recipes to enjoy at home
World.content:
We're often told breakfast is "the most important meal of the day", but it's rarely given the time and energy we devote to lunch and dinner.

These delicious morning options are for when you do want something that requires a little more effort than a quick slice of toast.

From shakshuka to hotcakes, you can enjoy an indulgent breakfast or brunch at home with one of these recipes.

This puffed pancake bakes in the oven, making it a simple yet special breakfast. (ABC News: Thalia Ho)

This easy baked breakfast is the perfect addition to a lazy weekend.

There's no hovering over the hot plate with a spatula and the batter is quickly mixed with a blender or food processor.

You can also can make the most of some of autumn's best seasonal produce when caramelising apples or pears.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

You can adjust the number or eggs in this recipe to your liking. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

Eggs for breakfast is hardly groundbreaking territory, but this shakshuka is something a little more exciting and flavourful.

It's enhanced by spices such as cumin and paprika and served with fresh herbs and crumbled feta, and can be easily doubled if you're cooking for a crowd.

Add chilli flakes, cayenne pepper or fresh chopped chilli if you prefer your shakshuka spicy.

Baked French toast served with raspberries, maple syrup and mascarpone is an easy recipe for entertaining. (ABC News: Annika Kafcaloudis)

This baked French toast is an indulgent but hands-off weekend option.

It begins the night before and while some work is required in the morning, it's a much simpler alternative to individually frying French toast for family brunch.

Serve with plenty of maple syrup.

Top your rice porridge with crispy fried egg, chilli and sesame for a punchy, flavour-packed twist. (ABC TV: Wesley Mitton)

Rice breaks down into a creamy porridge-like consistency in this savoury and naturally gluten-free breakfast.

This variation of congee or juk includes kimchi, spring onions, ginger and a crispy fried egg, but can be adjusted to your flavour preference.

World.title: Hasrat's life changed the day she stumbled across the T20 World Cup
World.content:
Hasrat Gill's earliest memories of cricket are like a lot of Australian kids.

She grew up in the backyard with either a bat and ball in hand and then would head inside, where Test cricket was regularly on the TV.

Then one day in 2016, when she was 10, she was flicking through channels on the TV and came across the Women's T20 World Cup in India.

"For the first time in my life, I actually realised that girls played cricket," Gill, who was born in India, tells ABC Sport.

Before that, she had predominantly played with boys at her primary school, as her fellow female classmates were not that interested in learning how to bowl.

But watching Indian captain Mithali Raj and star player Harmanpreet Kaur on the TV planted seeds in her brain.

"That was the moment where I was like, 'You know what? I really want to play cricket now because I can see that there's a pathway for young girls to follow,'" she says.

Indian-born Australian Hasrat Gill has represented Australia in the Under-19 Women’s squad. (Getty: Alex Davidson-ICC/ICC)

It helps, too, that she has always been naturally gifted.

"It's funny because when I was younger, I just thought anyone could run in and bowl with a straight arm," she laughs.

Gill, now 20, is an all-rounder for Victoria's state team and plays for Sydney Thunder after entering the WBBL at just 16 when she first signed with the Melbourne Stars.

And after donning the green and gold at the 2025 ICC Under-19 Women's T20 World Cup, and playing next to the likes of Meg Lanning and Phoebe Litchfield, she's now firmly "jumped ship" to supporting Australia as her number one team now.

Gill's rise through the Australian cricketing ranks has been against a backdrop of South Asian teenagers gravitating towards the sport.

Australia's cricket boom Australian cricket is booming at junior levels but as the sport attracts a more diverse and higher player base, the pressure on some of these kids is becoming too much and burnout looms.

Cricket has rapidly emerged as the first-choice, premier sport for South Asian teenagers in Australia, with massive participation surges at the grassroots level.

Driven by cultural heritage and high engagement, South Asian youth make up a significant portion —up to 40 per cent in some age groups — of junior cricket, often overtaking traditional Australian sports like soccer, Aussie Rules or rugby.

This year, Victoria has seen a further 5 per cent year-on-year increase in South Asian participation, driven in part by a 20 per cent uptick in junior cricket and 16 per cent increase in women's and girl's participation.

Gill is not surprised by those numbers.

Hasrat Gill has loved cricket since she was a kid. (Getty: Josh Chadwick)

She was born in Amritsar, the second-largest city in Punjab and was raised by her grandparents for the first two and a half years of her life while her parents sorted her visa for Australia.

For her, it is the visibility piece of having high-profile players like Usman Khawaja and Alana King at the top, while at the grassroots, the sport is a cultural heritage connector back to countries like India and Pakistan.

"You're seeing a lot of second-generation immigrants as well … I think that's a general trend across the state because we've got a really strong South Asian community in Victoria," Gill says, adding Cricket Australia has done a lot of work with their multicultural plan to appeal to different communities.

"It's a flow-on effect … and being such a big part of Indian culture, I think it's a natural sort of transition.

" Humans are herd animals and we like to feel like we belong. So I feel naturally that you will gravitate towards things that represent or reflect your own beliefs. "

While different league executives grapple with how to make their sport the most desired amongst the country's youth, Gill hopes to see more South Asian representation across the board.

The next step in South Asian inclusion in Australian sport, for her, would be more representation in codes like soccer and AFL.

"There's obviously so much more that can be done," Gill says.

"But also it's important to remember how far things have come already."

Hasrat Gill now plays for Sydney Thunder. (Getty: Adam Trafford)

Gill is not shy about wanting to play for Australia one day. Her "big goal, the ambitious goal" is to not just make the team but consistently represent her country.

"For myself personally, I don't want to just be someone that's just another player that's played domestic cricket, like there's so many of those around, and there's nothing wrong with that. That's what you want to do, of course," she says.

"But for me, like, from my perspective, and seeing how things are progressing in the women's game. You just want to be a part of it as much as you possibly can."

World.title: First Nations man dies in Queensland prison
World.content:
Police are preparing a report for the coroner after the death of a First Nations man in a Far North Queensland prison.

The 27-year-old inmate at the Lotus Glen Correctional Centre died on May 1, according to Queensland Corrective Services.

A spokesperson said the department was working with police to prepare a report for the coroner.

"This is standard practice for all deaths in custody," they said in a statement.

"While investigations are underway it would not be appropriate to comment further.

"Support is available to the responding officers and their colleagues."

Queensland Police said the death of the Normanton man was not suspicious.

Approximately 70 per cent of Lotus Glen's prison population are First Nations, according to the Queensland government.

The Lotus Glen facility houses more than 400 prisoners. (Supplied: Queeensland Corrective Services)

There have been 56 deaths in custody in Australia so far this year.

Indigenous people accounted for fourteen of those deaths, according to the Australian Institute of Criminology.

In 2024-25 Australia recorded the highest number of Indigenous deaths in custody in four decades.

World.title: Lucky endangered quoll survives 600km hitchhike in Qld
World.content:
The last place you would expect to spot an endangered northern quoll is in the wheel arch of a truck in Brisbane.

But that's exactly what happened when one of the carnivorous marsupials accidentally hitchhiked more than 600 kilometres from Rockhampton to south-east Queensland.

The Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI) today said members of public had noticed the animal fleeing the truck and contacted a wildlife carer, who was able to capture it from a nearby home.

Senior wildlife ranger Leigh Deutscher said the truck driver would have been unaware the quoll had been hiding somewhere on board during the transit in March.

Wildlife rangers say it was lucky the travelling quoll wasn't hurt. (Supplied: DETSI)

"It's a very lucky quoll on multiple fronts," Mr Deutscher said.

"One, that it managed to survive that journey and then also that it was spotted by someone and they were able to get the relevant authorities to pick it up and look after it," he said.

"We are not sure the exact origin of the truck … but the best we could get was that it was from Rockhampton, so that's where we had a look at the existing populations and where it would be most suitable to release it."

Northern quolls can be found in parts of Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia and are susceptible to cane toad toxins, fires and introduced predators such as foxes and cats.

They are protected under the Nature Conservation Act in Queensland and are listed as an endangered species under the Commonwealth Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act.

The travelling quoll was taken to the Currumbin Wildlife Hospital on the Gold Coast for assessment and monitoring, where senior veterinarian Michael Pyne found it was surprisingly healthy.

"While he wasn't thrilled with living with us, he ate very well and settled in nicely in hospital life," Dr Pyne said.

"He was with us for about a week. We had an initial detailed examination and then it was just waiting to work out how to get him back towards Rockhampton."

The animal was released back into bushland on the outskirts of Rockhampton, where there is a small population of quolls. (Supplied: DETSI)

The marsupial was then driven back to Rockhampton by DETSI staff.

Wildlife rangers found a suitable bushland location on the outskirts of the city with an established population of quolls for it to be released.

"There's a couple of quoll populations; they are pretty fragmented in our region unfortunately due to threats. They've become somewhat limited in terms of numbers," Mr Deutscher said.

"That's why it's really important that this little fella, we were able to get him back because having those quolls, particularly given they are a short-lived species, maintaining that genetic diversity is very important."

Mr Deutscher said it was not the first time northern quolls had been reported in built-up areas around central Queensland.

"We have had records previously about quolls being in Rockhampton and getting into people's chicken coops," he said.

"There have been records of them in Rosslyn near Yeppoon. There was one found there a few years back but unfortunately it was roadkill."

Anyone who finds sick, injured or orphaned wildlife is encouraged to contact the RSPCA on 1300 ANIMAL.

World.title: Sunwater CEO Glenn Stockton resigns amid dam controversy
World.content:
Sunwater chief executive officer Glenn Stockton has resigned amid new turmoil surrounding Queensland's troubled Paradise Dam.

The ABC understands Mr Stockton left the water service provider on Friday, just days before media reports revealed the board had advised the state government to abandon a $4.4 billion plan to rebuild the dam.

In a statement, the chair of Sunwater, Jeff Seeney, thanked Mr Stockton for almost six years of leadership.

“On behalf of the board, I offer Glenn our thanks for his dedication to Sunwater and he leaves with our best wishes for the future,” he said.

Mr Seeney said a formal recruitment process to appoint his replacement would begin immediately.

"Sunwater's commitments to its customers will continue to be the key focus of the organisation as it provides services to more than 4600 agriculture, urban and industrial clients," Mr Seeney said.

Paradise Dam turmoil

The announcement of Mr Stockton's departure came a day after the leaked details of the board's advice to abandon the $4.4 billion plan to rebuild the dam were reported.

Bundaberg's Paradise Dam wall was lowered due to safety issues. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

In a letter to Water Minister Ann Leahy, Mr Seeney said the previous government's pre-emptive announcement to "effectively abandon the existing Paradise Dam and build a new wall downstream was unsupported by the range of technical and financial information that would ordinarily be considered".

Mr Seeney said projected future water demand in the area supplied by Paradise Dam could be met by the current dam in its reduced height capacity "well past 2065".

Problems with the dam first emerged following the 2013 floods, with the then-Labor state government announcing it was lowering the dam wall by 5.8 metres in 2020 due to safety concerns.

Flood damage to the wall of Paradise Dam, near Bundaberg, in 2013. (ABC News: Supplied: Sunwater)

In 2023, Sunwater revealed degradation of the concrete had compromised the wall to the point that no amount of work could fix it.

The Miles government then committed to rebuilding the dam downstream, which the Crisafulli government also committed to when it was elected in 2024.

Revelations anger farmers

The latest revelations have angered the agriculture sector.

Bundaberg farmer and irrigator Judy Plath said the government should not need a business case to see the significant impact farming has on the region.

"To try to put that on a piece of paper completely disregards the hundreds of millions of dollars of investment that farmers have made in this district on the back of water security," she said.

Grower Judy Plath wants Paradise Dam restored to its full capacity. (ABC News: ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

The LNP Member for Burnett, Stephen Bennett, said the Crisafulli government remained committed to restoring water security for the region.

“Sunwater has raised concerns about the former Labor government’s disregard for process and taxpayers’ money," he said.

" My commitment to our community and our farmers has not changed and that is to restore water security for our region. "

Sunwater is due to deliver a detailed business case on the project by the end of the month.

World.title: 'Reward allies, remove critics': Ex-council CEO under ICAC spotlight
World.content:
The corruption watchdog is investigating whether the former CEO of City of Parramatta Council subverted hiring practices to purge "critics" and hire friends.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) commenced public hearings on Monday into allegations against former chief executive Gail Connolly and other employees that were hired during her two-and-a-half year tenure.

Ms Connolly, an otherwise celebrated public servant who held executive positions at Ryde City Council and Georges River Council, was appointed to lead City of Parramatta Council in April 2023 — earning more than $500,000 a year until councillors terminated her employment in October 2025.

Gail Connolly was appointed to lead the council in April 2023, with her employment terminated in October 2025. (Supplied: City of Parramatta Council)

Counsel Assisting the ICAC, Joanna Davidson SC, said the inquiry focused on the potentially illegal ways employees were surveilled, removed and replaced at the council.

"This inquiry is not concerned with ordinary managerial disagreement, or the robust exercise of executive authority," she said in her opening statement.

" Rather, it examines whether official decisions, council systems and access to confidential information were used in substance for partial and improper purposes, including to reward allies and remove critics or perceived opponents. "

From 2022 to 2025, City of Parramatta Council paid $5.2 million to more than 80 employees who were either fired or made redundant, though the ICAC hearing is focusing on a shorter period which Ms Connolly oversaw.

Covert electronic surveillance under question

The ICAC heard Ms Connolly's vendetta was set into motion in March 2023, a month before she was scheduled to start as chief executive, when there was a failed attempt to reportedly rescind her employment at an extraordinary council meeting.

"The rescission motion marked an early line between those staff perceived as supporters of the new CEO and those perceived as opponents," Ms Davidson said.

"This is a divide that it is alleged later influenced both scrutiny and reprisal."

The inquiry will focus on the legally questionable ways employees were surveilled, removed and replaced at the council. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

Ms Connolly and some subordinates allegedly used covert electronic surveillance and workplace investigations to help them gain an advantage in removing employees from their roles.

"These allegations raise serious questions concerning the lawful use of surveillance powers and compliance with [the law]," Ms Davidson said.

'Pink Ops' WhatsApp group

Within months of entering the job, Ms Connolly brought on two former colleagues and friends into high-paying executive roles — Roxanne Thornton as chief governance and risk officer, and Angela Jones-Blayney as executive director of city engagement.

City of Parramatta Council staff Roxanne Thornton, left, and Angela Jones-Blayney, right. (Supplied)

Ms Davidson said it was alleged the three women abused their roles to subvert hiring practices, making it easier for their friends and associates to secure work at the council, including by failing to disclose their relationships to the candidates.

"The number of occasions upon which this occurred gives rise to concerns as to whether the conduct was systemic," she said.

Many of the people hired — though not all of them — were part of a WhatsApp group titled 'Pink Ops', which Ms Davidson said played on the term 'Black Ops'.

She listed examples to illustrate the close relationship between Ms Connolly and Ms Thornton, who regularly holidayed together.

"During their time at Georges River Council, they controlled a Facebook profile under a name not belonging to either of them to comment on particular council-related matters," she said.

Counsel assisting also said Ms Connolly signed Ms Thornton's name when she needed a witness on her employment contract with City of Parramatta Council.

Interview questions given in advance

The commission heard Ms Connolly helped Ms Thornton secure her first role, and allowed her to help create a future position.

The hiring practices surrounding Ms Thornton's appointment are being reviewed by ICAC. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

A month after Ms Connolly joined the council, the head of legal services was made redundant.

The new position that was created assumed his team and did not require a law degree — at the alleged insistence of Ms Connolly.

The successful applicant for the 12-month role was Ms Thornton.

"Ms Connolly reviewed Ms Thornton's resume in preparation … and then failed to adequately declare a conflict of interest," Ms Davidson said.

Later, the commission heard Ms Thornton helped create the organisational structure that would include a future position (group manager — Office of the Lord Mayor and CEO), which she ultimately took up in February 2024.

"Ms Thornton was provided with a copy of the interview questions prior to her interview, as well as a copy of the interview guide for the position, which related to criteria for the assessment of candidates," Ms Davidson said.

She said the questions could have come from two people: Ms Connolly or her executive officer Anna Swanwick.

Ms Connolly also participated in the interview panel, the commission heard, disclosing the two had worked together but not mentioning their ongoing friendship.

The counsel assisting said the subversion of hiring practices could be systemic, with Ms Connolly similarly helping Ms Jones-Blayney.

Ms Davidson then provided five examples when Ms Thornton and Ms Jones-Blayney similarly helped other friends and associates land a job at the council.

Avoided putting things in writing

The hearing related to City of Parramatta Council will continue over the next four weeks. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

The ICAC heard Ms Connolly became paranoid about leaks to the media.

She deliberately avoided creating paper trails and correspondents from her work email address.

Instead, she allegedly would send work emails from her private account to other council staff.

"The lack of transparency was exacerbated by Ms Connolly's preference to avoid things put in writing," Ms Davidson said.

"Seemingly in an effort to avoid GIPA [freedom of information] requests and also, because of what some of the evidence available to the Commission has described as ultimately 'an atmosphere of paranoia'."

The hearing will continue over the next four weeks.

World.title: ‘Australia’s flame-haired answer to Farage’: How One Nation’s win has played out overseas
World.content:
PoliticsFederalByelection ‘Australia’s flame-haired answer to Farage’: How One Nation’s win has played out overseas Staff reporter May 11, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation’s thumping victory in Saturday’s Farrer byelection has made headlines overseas, foreign media having highlighted leader Pauline Hanson’s admiration for US President Donald Trump and the growing electoral support globally for far-right populist parties. Hanson’s candidate, David Farley, wrested the regional NSW electorate from Coalition hands for the first time in its 77-year history, delivering One Nation its first lower house seat in an election in its three-decade history. A triumphant Hanson promised her minor party would seize on the momentum to deliver action on a gas tax and lower immigration. One Nation’s victory in the Farrer byelection has put Pauline Hanson and her successful use of Trumpian rhetoric on the global map. Marija Ercegovac London’s Telegraph has been the most dramatic in its coverage, saying Australia’s mainstream political parties have been put on notice by the country’s “flame-haired answer to [Nigel] Farage”, whose right-wing Reform UK party delivered a catastrophic defeat to the governing Labour Party and the Conservatives in local elections last week. Just like Hanson’s fans in Australia, the voters in the UK have rallied to Farage’s call for a hard line on migration and welfare, the paper said. “Reminiscent of Mr Farage, Ms Hanson is a one-woman show who has capitalised on discontent in traditional parties, triggered by the cost of living and mass migration,” the Telegraph said.



“Like Mr Farage, Ms Hanson has been a staunch supporter of Donald Trump, even when his policies bordered on hostile acts against her country.” Related Article Analysis

UK ‘A horrible place’: This gloomy town shows why angry voters are lurching to the right And like Farage’s Reform UK, One Nation might not need backing from the mainstream if its rise continued before the federal election, the Telegraph said. Hanson’s love for Trump and his brand of right-wing populist rhetoric has also been the key focus of The New York Times’ coverage of One Nation’s win in Farrer. Many of Hanson’s positions were closely aligned with Trump’s messaging, the paper said, adding that she praised the US president’s policies and said she wanted to mirror them in Australia when she spoke last year at the Conservative Political Action Conference at Mar-a-Lago, in Florida.



In her victory speech on Saturday, she struck a Trumpian note, the Times reported. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Hanson attacks Coalition at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago as she closes on Ley in polls “I don’t want Shariah law on our doorstep. I want true people that want to come on board to be Australians, and join us in this journey of making our country the greatest country in the world again,” it quoted Hanson as saying at her party’s celebration. While drawing parallels with the growing popularity of right-wing politics in Europe, the Times’ coverage did point out the sketchy political track record of One Nation. “At the same time, the populist surge in Australia is not yet at the levels seen in Britain, and One Nation has a checkered history when it comes to keeping the party together and organising on a national level, raising questions about whether it can endure as a movement,” the newspaper said, citing Frank Bongiorno, a historian and professor at the University of Canberra.



Pauline Hanson embraces a supporter at the One Nation HQ party in Albury on Saturday. Janie Barrett The BBC said the result was a clear sign that voters were moving away from traditional political parties in Australia, and a test for new Liberal leader Angus Taylor and new Nationals leader Matt Canavan. Taylor’s party recorded a paltry 12 per cent of the vote in a seat it had held for 25 years. Elsewhere, Al Jazeera said while Farley’s victory did little to affect the balance in the lower house of parliament, it was in line with growing electoral support for far-right populist parties globally. World.title: Bystanders praised as woman behind alleged antisemitic netball slur named
World.content:
Bystanders who confronted a woman who allegedly hurled an antisemitic slur at an under 12s Jewish netball team have been praised for speaking up by one community leader who said “such incidents occur all the time”. It comes as the woman accused of marring the Sydney eastern suburbs’ competition has been identified as a suburban Sydney mum. Jody Scarcella allegedly made antisemitic comments during a children’s netball match at Maroubra. alexryvchin Jody Scarcella, 42, was banned by NSW Netball from attending any courts or games after police received reports of “offensive comments” during a match between Maccabi Netball Club and Saints Netball Club. Police were called to the match at Heffron Park in Maroubra on Saturday. Officers did not arrest Scarcella but charged her with using offensive language near a school or public place.



Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin, who arrived at the courts shortly after the incident, said the woman had said “F--- the Jews” and suggested they should be “eradicated”. “What makes this incident unique is not the element of serious racial abuse or that it was done in a family setting in the presence of kids. Such incidents occur all the time,” Ryvchin told this masthead. Alex Ryvchin said the abuse allegedly happened in “plain sight”. Wolter Peeters “It was unique because those directly affected by it stood up to it, took appropriate action, and held this person to account.” Ryvchin said it was obvious that society is “becoming angrier, more polarised and more violent”.



Those who behave “appallingly” should face the consequences, he added. Related Article Antisemitism Mother charged after police called to netball game over antisemitic incident “The vast majority don’t need hate speech laws or the threat of life bans to know you don’t utter racist slurs during an under 12s netball game. But those who think it’s OK, need to see that people will stand up to them and they’re not going to get away with it any longer,” he said. “A line was drawn that morning and hopefully it now forces people to think before they speak, and it spares others from going through such an ugly experience.” Scarcella told the Herald she did not want to comment, but said she was “scared”.



The Chifley woman is a member of the South Maroubra Surf Life Saving Club, according to an annual report. She will appear at Waverley court on June 17. President of Maccabi Netball Club Adam Dinte called the incident “completely unacceptable”. Police were called to the match at Heffron Park in Maroubra on Saturday. “We are aware of a deeply distressing antisemitic incident that occurred at a netball game today involving Jewish players and families from our club,” Dinte said in a statement to club members.



“We are taking this matter extremely seriously. “Maccabi NSW is communicating with NSW Police and the Community Security Group [CSG]. We are also writing a formal letter of complaint to the Randwick Netball Association and the opposing club. “Jewish players, parents, coaches, administrators and supporters have the right to participate in community sport safely and confidently, free from racism, abuse, intimidation or vilification.” The general manager of Maccabi Australia, the umbrella body of Australian Jewish Sport, David Goldman, said the incident was “tragic and disturbing” but was not isolated.



Related Article Opinion

Antisemitism I reported on antisemitism, but then it hit me first-hand – at my daughter’s netball game Alexandra Smith Senior writer He noted that a recent survey of 670 Maccabi members found nearly one in two respondents had either witnessed or experienced antisemitism in sport. “This isn’t isolated to Sydney, and it’s not isolated to netball. It’s occurred across other sporting codes, and we’ve seen certainly a spike in incident since October 7,” Goldman said. Maccabi Australia chief executive Mandy Penkin said the alleged incident was “horrifying” but “unsurprising”. “It’s just absolutely shocking that in a country like Australia, at an under-12 netball game, that kids should not feel comfortable to play sport wearing the Jewish colours for fear of being abused,” Penkin said. “The fact that we see it pop up so often is heartbreaking.”



David Ossip, president of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, said the incident must be “swiftly investigated” and there must be no tolerance for racism and discrimination. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump is snookered on Iran. Walking away may be his least worst option
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump is snookered on Iran. Walking away may be his least worst option Michael Koziol May 11, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Iran has delivered its response to the US’s one-page pitch for peace, and it’s not good. “I don’t like it – TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE!” was Donald Trump’s appraisal of the Iranians’ position. Quelle surprise. US intelligence agencies are analysing the consequences of Donald Trump simply declaring mission accomplished in Iran and drawing down troops. AP For weeks, the US president has teased of an imminent deal with Iran to end the war, based on the claim that Iran has been summarily defeated on the battlefield; its air force destroyed and its navy at the bottom of the gulf.



Experts on Iran, however, have consistently warned that military victory does not necessarily translate to strategic triumph. They have argued that Trump and his coterie of diplomatic novices fundamentally misunderstand the Iranian regime – which, contrary to their assertions, still stands. Related Article Middle East at war ‘I don’t like it’: Trump blasts Iran’s ‘unacceptable’ response to US proposal to end war One often extends Trump the benefit of the doubt – he has humbled the foreign policy establishment before – but only for so long. Despite the US turning the screws on Tehran with a naval blockade and a new wave of economic sanctions, the regime is not buckling. “Iran does not believe it lost this confrontation,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch of the Israeli military’s intelligence unit. “Iran has no intention of capitulating or accepting Washington’s demands – not now, and not in the foreseeable future.”



That leaves Trump with three choices: make a suite of ugly concessions that would leave him accused of settling for a deal worse than Barack Obama’s 2015 agreement with Iran, restart the bombing in the hope of ousting the regime or forcing a better deal, or simply walking away. Trump has certainly laid the groundwork for the latter. We have heard him say over and over that the war has been won, the Iranian regime has been changed – and even more explicitly, that if the US left now, it would take Iran 20 years to rebuild. Loading There was also a Reuters report two weeks ago that said US intelligence agencies were analysing the likely consequences of Trump simply declaring mission accomplished and drawing down troops. That might be the least worst option. The US could credibly say it inflicted a lot of damage and set back Iran’s nuclear ambitions again, while reserving the right to revisit the matter down the track.





While always keeping on the table further military action, Trump has been reluctant to go down that path. Not only is the war unpopular with Americans, but he would have to answer the question of what fresh strikes would achieve that was not achieved in the first 37 days of intense bombing. Related Article China relations The five ‘Bs’ and three ‘Ts’ at the heart of the Trump-Xi meeting By delaying its inevitably unsatisfactory response, which was initially going to come last week, Iran has also forced Trump into an awkward position in the days before his important trip to China. Restarting strikes could jeopardise the visit. But arriving in Beijing without a credible path forward and asking Chinese President Xi Jinping for help in corralling the Iranians looks weak. A senior US official said Trump would probably pressure Xi to curb the sale of dual-use components and potential weapons to Iran, as he had done in the past.



“I expect that conversation to continue,” the official said on a phone call with reporters on Sunday (US time). “You’ve seen some actions, meaning sanctions, coming out from the US side in the last few days that I’m sure will be part of that conversation. “I would expect the president to apply pressure … he has done so before.” View post on X Vali Nasr, an Iran expert and professor of international affairs at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland, noted that applying such pressure on Xi would not be easy. The Chinese would seek to extract something in return for their help, Nasr said on X – and they could still say no. The Beijing summit would then be “another casualty of the war”. World.title: State clears 70 per cent of DNA backlog, returns to testing in July
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government State clears 70 per cent of DNA backlog, returns to testing in July Catherine Strohfeldt May 11, 2026 — 3:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A backlog of 600 samples linked to rape investigations in Queensland has been cleared by the state laboratory following the DNA bungle that botched testing of samples from thousands of major crimes. Attorney-general Deb Frecklington said the state had increased the number of scientists from 19 to 24 at the state lab, Forensic Science Queensland, and appointed two new members to its leadership board. She said the state had also cleared 70 per cent of samples from major crimes that had been awaiting testing since November – equating to more than 8200 samples. Forensic Science Queensland and former NSW police commissioner Mick Fuller. Catherine Strohfeldt “These aren’t just numbers, these are people who were waiting and left waiting,” Frecklington said.



Related Article Queensland government Qld’s ‘dirty lab’ leaves rape victims at risk of further assault: report The lab has been in a perpetual state of scandal since late 2021 and the centre of two landmark commissions of inquiry after former forensic biologist Dr Kirsty Wright blew the whistle on alleged testing failures in the 2013 murder investigation of Shandee Blackburn. FSQ is a statutory authority established to respond to the bungle in 2023 following revelations cracks in Queensland’s then automated DNA extraction method might have led to offenders escaping conviction from 2007 to 2016. However, a report released in June indicated that from early 2023, scientists had knowingly been testing samples in a “dirty lab”, meaning some results given to police and used to prosecute cases were unreliable. In late 2025, the state began outsourcing testing to United States forensics laboratory Bode Technology.





“The goal [of] mine is to restart the sexual assault testing in probably July this year, which means that we could be turning around results within five or 10 working days,” he said. The state had also retested results for about 20,000 previously analysed samples, from an initial 40,000 that fell within the scope of a historical review process. In June last year, the lab had tested 10,000 of the flagged samples. Fuller previously said he expected the state could clear about 1000 major crime samples and 175 forensic medical examination kits per month but reiterated on Monday clearing the backlog would take “an enormous amount of time”. “It’s just not about grabbing a vial and retesting – you really have to look at continuity of all aspects of it, but we are reducing it,” he said.



The two new FSQ leadership members include UK Metropolitan Police forensic scientist Saranjeet Khera and long-time Justice Department worker Kirsten Eades. Shadow Attorney-General Meaghan Scanlon said on Monday the backlog had begun to be reduced under the former Labor government. “Ultimately some of these issues have been over a long period of time over both sides of politics, and I think everyone wants to see justice delivered to victims of crime, and this really should be a bipartisan issue,” she told reporters outside Parliament House. World.title: Zenith bags missing link to unite 6km WA gold corridor
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Zenith bags missing link to unite 6km WA gold corridor Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS May 11, 2026 — 3:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Zenith Minerals has officially secured the “missing link” at its flagship Consolidated Dulcie gold project in Western Australia, completing the acquisition of a crucial mining lease that unites its gold-rich tenure into one continuous six-kilometre mineralised corridor. The formal registration of the mining lease marks the first time the company has held total control over the primary trend, effectively plugging a 600-metre gap between its two main gold deposits. Zenith Minerals’ newly granted and strategically placed mining lease M77/599 fills in the final piece of the company’s Dulcie gold project near Marvel Loch in Western Australia. The strategically vital piece of real estate sits directly between Zenith’s Dulcie North and Dulcie deposits. While the fresh ground remains largely untested by the drill bit, the gold signature on either side is remarkably consistent. To the north, Dulcie North hosts 75,000 ounces of gold over a 500-metre strike, while to the south, the main Dulcie deposit clocks 300,000 ounces of gold across a three-kilometre strike, both in the inferred category. The company says this central corridor position represents one of the most compelling near-resource growth opportunities within the broader project area.



“For the first time, Zenith now controls the full ~6 kilometre strike extent of the Dulcie mineralised corridor.′ Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith According to management, there is clear potential to link mineralisation between the existing deposits and materially expand the current global resource at Consolidated Dulcie, which stands at 21.3 million tonnes grading 1.0 gram per tonne (g/t) gold for 675,000 ounces of gold. Crucially, the broader system remains open both along strike and at depth. With the fresh ground secured, the company will now charge ahead with preparations for a planned 35-hole reverse circulation drilling program. The company says technical and permitting work is well advanced, with flora and fauna surveys, aerial digital terrain model acquisition and drill planning already substantially progressed. Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith said: “We believe this tenure has the potential to materially enhance the scale and continuity of the Consolidated Dulcie Gold project and provides a highly compelling near-term drilling opportunity.” The 5000-metre campaign is specifically designed to test the continuity of the stacked, shallow-dipping lode system across the company’s freshly acquired ground between deposits.



The Consolidated Dulcie project sits within the Southern Cross–Forrestania gold belt and benefits from granted mining leases, shallow open-pit style mineralisation and proximity to regional processing infrastructure at Marvel Loch and Edna May. Elsewhere, Zenith’s exploration plays include its promising Red Mountain gold project in Queensland. Recent diamond drilling has now plumbed the depths of gold mineralisation beyond 700 metres vertical depth at the prospect, reinforcing the continuity of a broad breccia-hosted intrusion-related gold system (IRGS) at depth. Among its standout results, one hole ending at 731m downhole depth returned a best intercept of 333m grading 0.27g/t gold from 388m downhole. The intersection also encountered narrow high-grade veins of 2m at 6.55g/t gold and 2.2m at 4.16g/t gold. The company also holds a 25 per cent free-carried interest in the Earaheedy zinc project in one of Western Australia’s premier undeveloped zinc districts. The portfolio is rounded out by an active stake in the Cowarra gold project in New South Wales and its Split Rocks lithium project near Southern Cross in WA, host to an inferred resource of 11.9 million tonnes at 0.72 per cent lithium oxide. As the company kicks off its fresh drilling program, it is also navigating a formal strategic review aimed at closing the gap between its share price and its underlying asset value.



Financial advisers are now on deck, with inbound interest already noted. Zenith says the next few months will be about proving up the full scale of the Dulcie trend and determining the best corporate pathway to unlock its maximum value. With the full six kilometres of the Dulcie trend finally under one roof and the drill rigs ready to roll, Zenith now appears well-positioned to prove exactly what its WA gold hub is worth. It is a classic “connect the dots” play that could turn a series of deposits into a serious production powerhouse. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.title: Noah Lolesio is keen to stay in Japan. He knows it could cost him a World Cup berth
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Noah Lolesio is keen to stay in Japan. He knows it could cost him a World Cup berth Jonathan Drennan May 11, 2026 — 3:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies five-eighth Noah Lolesio wants to extend his stay in Japan, but acknowledged his continued absence from Australia could jeopardise his immediate Test hopes. Places for overseas-based Wallabies have grown tighter after RA director of high-performance Peter Horne told this masthead the governing body still uses the 2022 iteration of its policy on overseas players, dubbed the “Giteau Law”, which allows just three players based outside Australia to be selected. Noah Lolesio is keen to extend his time in Japan Getty Images Lolesio starred on Sunday for his Japanese side Toyota Industries Shuttles Aichi in a 34-27 win against Kintetsu Liners, scoring a try and kicking eight points to help his team clinch the division two title and a place in the promotion playoff later this month. Lolesio originally signed for one year in Japan, with an option to extend his stay for a second season. The 26-year-old suffered a serious neck injury last July in the Test against Fiji ahead of the British and Irish Lions series, fearing at one stage he would be paralysed.



Lolesio has started ten games for Toyota Industries Shuttles Aichi, becoming a key figure in their promotion push. The playmaker has remained in close contact with Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt and hasn’t given up hope of a Test recall. “Getting these boys promoted to division one would play a huge factor [in staying] ... playing rugby here in Japan is definitely something that I’ll be keen to do,” Lolesio said. Mark Nawaqanitawase caught up with Noah Lolesio recently ahead of his move to Japan next season Getty Images “Obviously, through my form and performances here in Japan, I do hope to get the call-up with the Wallabies. It’s a massive honour to put on that gold jersey. But at the same time, I completely understand if they select the boys playing back home, because they’re playing good footy as well. “It’s probably a good problem to have. There are a lot of good fly-halves in Australia.”



Lolesio is enjoying life in the small city of Kariya and has graduated from Google Translate to holding conversations in basic Japanese with teammates and locals. Lolesio recently caught up with Roosters winger Mark Nawaqanitawase in Bondi to brief him on what to expect ahead of his move to Saitama Wild Knights in Division One. “I literally just saw him in Sydney a few weeks ago, and I had a good catch-up with him,” Lolesio said. “He’s really excited and I couldn’t be happier for him. I was just telling him what it’s like over here, but honestly, there’s no stress about him, he’ll thrive here and will do a really good job for his team.” Lolesio on Sunday faced Springboks playmaker Manie Libbok, now plying his trade at the Liners, and insists the standard in Japan’s division two is higher than many realise.



“I feel like definitely the misconception is that it’s easy,” Lolesio said. “It’s definitely not, I can tell you that right now. I think that’s probably the biggest thing that boys back home think, [that] they can just come here and park up and just let things happen. “But there are a lot of different challenges that come with playing in Japan. It’s just something completely different. It’s really hard to explain, but you just have to be here to experience it. Lolesio suffered a serious neck injury in the Test against Fiji last July. AP “Returning back to Australia eventually is the plan for me, I’m young now, so I can experience all of this and then maybe one day, who knows when that is, but I’ll definitely be keen to return to Australia, wherever that is.” Meanwhile, Super Rugby has backed its officials after the Queensland Reds lodged a formal complaint with the competition over the standard of refereeing in their controversial loss to the Chiefs on Friday.



Related Article Reds TMO controversy sours Reds’ defeat, but McReight calls for player ‘ownership’ Reds second-rower Seru Uru looked to have scored a try shortly before half-time, but referee Marcus Playle ruled the ball was held up before seeking a TMO review. TMO Glenn Newman then took 26 seconds to decide there was no clear evidence to overturn the original decision, and the half-time whistle was blown. In a statement on Monday afternoon, Super Rugby backed the original decision from the officials and said Newman had viewed all the clear angles available to him. “Super Rugby Pacific management has reviewed the ‘held up’ decision involving Queensland Reds forward Seru Uru just prior to half-time in last Friday’s game between the Reds and Chiefs.



“It was confirmed the television match official (TMO) viewed all available angles of the play while reviewing the on-field decision. “The TMO identified evidence the ball had been grounded however could not find clear and obvious evidence the ball was grounded on or over the tryline, which would be required to overturn the on-field decision.” Watch every match of the 2026 Super Rugby Pacific season live and exclusive on Stan Sport.

World.title: An eclipse had just finished dazzling Exmouth when the phone at a remote WA roadhouse started ringing
World.content:
NationalWATourism An eclipse had just finished dazzling Exmouth when the phone at a remote WA roadhouse started ringing Holly Thompson May 11, 2026 — 3:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The moon had barely finished traversing its celestial path to block the sun in front of a crowd of almost 20,000 people in Exmouth in 2023 when the phones started ringing off the hook at a remote roadhouse in the Kimberley. Doon Doon, around 100 kilometres south of Kununurra, was named as the place to be when the next total solar eclipse was scheduled to cross WA’s north in July 2028. Doon Doon Roadhouse will be one of the best places to view the next solar eclipse in 2028. Facebook/Doon Doon Roadhouse Roadhouse manager Shayne Stewart said he had been contacted by multiple people wanting to book at their campsite and cabins, including one from America who asked to book out the entire place. While the roadhouse wasn’t able to take bookings until mid-2027, Stewart said they had recently added 40 new rooms and were already full, hosting fly-in, fly-out workers, travellers and truck drivers most of the year.



“We are looking at extending the campground to create 100 new unpowered sites, possibly more if we can for the eclipse,” he said. “We need to figure out the cost of everything, and the logistics around hosting a possible 2000 people. No one has made contact with us yet about funding. A total solar eclipse in Exmouth, Western Australia. Nine News “The Exmouth event had a whole town behind it – we are just a little roadhouse in the middle of nowhere.” Stewart said the big issues to address would be employing more staff to help out for such a short timeframe, feeding so many people, and building the infrastructure required.



Western Australia’s budget, released last week, revealed $24.6 million would be set aside to plan for an expected 25,000 additional visitors to the North and East Kimberley for the total solar eclipse, and the strain that will be placed on resources in the remote towns that dot the region. The Kimberley will experience more than four minutes of totality – when the moon completely eclipses the sun – on July 22, 2028, and will be one of the best places in the world to view the natural phenomenon. Related Article Space The WA coastal town bracing for 18,000 visitors - 10 times its population Stewart said the roadhouse was “smack bang in the centre” as the best viewing spot, and would experience totality for several minutes longer than other areas like Kununurra. Part of the funding from the budget – $13.2 million – will go towards planning and event management activities, including a planned Doon Doon viewing site, overflow accommodation facilities at Kununurra racecourse, and telecommunication upgrades.



The Water Corporation will receive $9.2 million to undertake “essential” water and wastewater upgrades in Kununurra to support additional visitation. Main Roads will also be given $1.1 million to upgrade roads at the Doon Doon viewing site, and Horizon Power has been promised $810,000 to upgrade power infrastructure at the Kununurra racecourse. On top of that, $272,000 has been approved for the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions for event management. In 2023, portable mobile phone towers and water tanks were installed in Exmouth town, and septic tanks were installed on the Ningaloo Coastal Reserve and at state camping sites to cope with the influx. Regional Development and Kimberley Minister Stephen Dawson said the Kimberley would be the “best place in the world” to see the astrological phenomenon, with the longest period of totality, clearest skies, and dramatic landscapes.



“The government is funding key infrastructure and services to enable visitors from across the country as well as from overseas to visit the region for this unique experience,” he said. “The event is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for residents and visitors, as well as providing an economic boost to local communities and businesses.” Kimberley MLA Divina D’Anna said it would also be an opportunity to showcase the beauty and uniqueness of the Kimberley to the world. “Investing over $24.6 million in legacy critical infrastructure upgrades and public safety services (will) prepare the region for this extraordinary event,” she said. “Improvements to camping sites, water facilities, and telecommunications will ensure a safe and memorable experience for all attending.”

World.title: ‘Australia’s flame-haired answer to Farage’: How One Nation’s win has played out overseas
World.content:
PoliticsFederalByelection ‘Australia’s flame-haired answer to Farage’: How One Nation’s win has played out overseas Staff reporter May 11, 2026 — 3:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation’s thumping victory in Saturday’s Farrer byelection has made headlines overseas, foreign media having highlighted leader Pauline Hanson’s admiration for US President Donald Trump and the growing electoral support globally for far-right populist parties. Hanson’s candidate, David Farley, wrested the regional NSW electorate from Coalition hands for the first time in its 77-year history, delivering One Nation its first lower house seat in an election in its three-decade history. A triumphant Hanson promised her minor party would seize on the momentum to deliver action on a gas tax and lower immigration. One Nation’s victory in the Farrer byelection has put Pauline Hanson and her successful use of Trumpian rhetoric on the global map. Marija Ercegovac London’s Telegraph has been the most dramatic in its coverage, saying Australia’s mainstream political parties have been put on notice by the country’s “flame-haired answer to [Nigel] Farage”, whose right-wing Reform UK party delivered a catastrophic defeat to the governing Labour Party and the Conservatives in local elections last week. Just like Hanson’s fans in Australia, the voters in the UK have rallied to Farage’s call for a hard line on migration and welfare, the paper said. “Reminiscent of Mr Farage, Ms Hanson is a one-woman show who has capitalised on discontent in traditional parties, triggered by the cost of living and mass migration,” the Telegraph said.



“Like Mr Farage, Ms Hanson has been a staunch supporter of Donald Trump, even when his policies bordered on hostile acts against her country.” Related Article Analysis

UK ‘A horrible place’: This gloomy town shows why angry voters are lurching to the right And like Farage’s Reform UK, One Nation might not need backing from the mainstream if its rise continued before the federal election, the Telegraph said. Hanson’s love for Trump and his brand of right-wing populist rhetoric has also been the key focus of The New York Times’ coverage of One Nation’s win in Farrer. Many of Hanson’s positions were closely aligned with Trump’s messaging, the paper said, adding that she praised the US president’s policies and said she wanted to mirror them in Australia when she spoke last year at the Conservative Political Action Conference at Mar-a-Lago, in Florida.



In her victory speech on Saturday, she struck a Trumpian note, the Times reported. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Hanson attacks Coalition at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago as she closes on Ley in polls “I don’t want Shariah law on our doorstep. I want true people that want to come on board to be Australians, and join us in this journey of making our country the greatest country in the world again,” it quoted Hanson as saying at her party’s celebration. While drawing parallels with the growing popularity of right-wing politics in Europe, the Times’ coverage did point out the sketchy political track record of One Nation. “At the same time, the populist surge in Australia is not yet at the levels seen in Britain, and One Nation has a checkered history when it comes to keeping the party together and organising on a national level, raising questions about whether it can endure as a movement,” the newspaper said, citing Frank Bongiorno, a historian and professor at the University of Canberra.



Pauline Hanson embraces a supporter at the One Nation HQ party in Albury on Saturday. Janie Barrett The BBC said the result was a clear sign that voters were moving away from traditional political parties in Australia, and a test for new Liberal leader Angus Taylor and new Nationals leader Matt Canavan. Taylor’s party recorded a paltry 12 per cent of the vote in a seat it had held for 25 years. Elsewhere, Al Jazeera said while Farley’s victory did little to affect the balance in the lower house of parliament, it was in line with growing electoral support for far-right populist parties globally. World.title: Bystanders praised as woman behind alleged antisemitic netball slur named
World.content:
Bystanders who confronted a woman who allegedly hurled an antisemitic slur at an under 12s Jewish netball team have been praised for speaking up by one community leader who said “such incidents occur all the time”. It comes as the woman accused of marring the Sydney eastern suburbs’ competition has been identified as a suburban Sydney mum. Jody Scarcella allegedly made antisemitic comments during a children’s netball match at Maroubra. alexryvchin Jody Scarcella, 42, was banned by NSW Netball from attending any courts or games after police received reports of “offensive comments” during a match between Maccabi Netball Club and Saints Netball Club. Police were called to the match at Heffron Park in Maroubra on Saturday. Officers did not arrest Scarcella but charged her with using offensive language near a school or public place.



Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin, who arrived at the courts shortly after the incident, said the woman had said “F--- the Jews” and suggested they should be “eradicated”. “What makes this incident unique is not the element of serious racial abuse or that it was done in a family setting in the presence of kids. Such incidents occur all the time,” Ryvchin told this masthead. Alex Ryvchin said the abuse allegedly happened in “plain sight”. Wolter Peeters “It was unique because those directly affected by it stood up to it, took appropriate action, and held this person to account.” Ryvchin said it was obvious that society is “becoming angrier, more polarised and more violent”.



Those who behave “appallingly” should face the consequences, he added. Related Article Antisemitism Mother charged after police called to netball game over antisemitic incident “The vast majority don’t need hate speech laws or the threat of life bans to know you don’t utter racist slurs during an under 12s netball game. But those who think it’s OK, need to see that people will stand up to them and they’re not going to get away with it any longer,” he said. “A line was drawn that morning and hopefully it now forces people to think before they speak, and it spares others from going through such an ugly experience.” Scarcella told the Herald she did not want to comment, but said she was “scared”.



The Chifley woman is a member of the South Maroubra Surf Life Saving Club, according to an annual report. She will appear at Waverley court on June 17. President of Maccabi Netball Club Adam Dinte called the incident “completely unacceptable”. Police were called to the match at Heffron Park in Maroubra on Saturday. “We are aware of a deeply distressing antisemitic incident that occurred at a netball game today involving Jewish players and families from our club,” Dinte said in a statement to club members.



“We are taking this matter extremely seriously. “Maccabi NSW is communicating with NSW Police and the Community Security Group [CSG]. We are also writing a formal letter of complaint to the Randwick Netball Association and the opposing club. “Jewish players, parents, coaches, administrators and supporters have the right to participate in community sport safely and confidently, free from racism, abuse, intimidation or vilification.” The general manager of Maccabi Australia, the umbrella body of Australian Jewish Sport, David Goldman, said the incident was “tragic and disturbing” but was not isolated.



Related Article Opinion

Antisemitism I reported on antisemitism, but then it hit me first-hand – at my daughter’s netball game Alexandra Smith Senior writer He noted that a recent survey of 670 Maccabi members found nearly one in two respondents had either witnessed or experienced antisemitism in sport. “This isn’t isolated to Sydney, and it’s not isolated to netball. It’s occurred across other sporting codes, and we’ve seen certainly a spike in incident since October 7,” Goldman said. Maccabi Australia chief executive Mandy Penkin said the alleged incident was “horrifying” but “unsurprising”. “It’s just absolutely shocking that in a country like Australia, at an under-12 netball game, that kids should not feel comfortable to play sport wearing the Jewish colours for fear of being abused,” Penkin said. “The fact that we see it pop up so often is heartbreaking.”



David Ossip, president of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, said the incident must be “swiftly investigated” and there must be no tolerance for racism and discrimination. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump is snookered on Iran. Walking away may be his least worst option
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump is snookered on Iran. Walking away may be his least worst option Michael Koziol May 11, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Iran has delivered its response to the US’s one-page pitch for peace, and it’s not good. “I don’t like it – TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE!” was Donald Trump’s appraisal of the Iranians’ position. Quelle surprise. US intelligence agencies are analysing the consequences of Donald Trump simply declaring mission accomplished in Iran and drawing down troops. AP For weeks, the US president has teased of an imminent deal with Iran to end the war, based on the claim that Iran has been summarily defeated on the battlefield; its air force destroyed and its navy at the bottom of the gulf.



Experts on Iran, however, have consistently warned that military victory does not necessarily translate to strategic triumph. They have argued that Trump and his coterie of diplomatic novices fundamentally misunderstand the Iranian regime – which, contrary to their assertions, still stands. Related Article Middle East at war ‘I don’t like it’: Trump blasts Iran’s ‘unacceptable’ response to US proposal to end war One often extends Trump the benefit of the doubt – he has humbled the foreign policy establishment before – but only for so long. Despite the US turning the screws on Tehran with a naval blockade and a new wave of economic sanctions, the regime is not buckling. “Iran does not believe it lost this confrontation,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former head of the Iran branch of the Israeli military’s intelligence unit. “Iran has no intention of capitulating or accepting Washington’s demands – not now, and not in the foreseeable future.”



That leaves Trump with three choices: make a suite of ugly concessions that would leave him accused of settling for a deal worse than Barack Obama’s 2015 agreement with Iran, restart the bombing in the hope of ousting the regime or forcing a better deal, or simply walking away. Trump has certainly laid the groundwork for the latter. We have heard him say over and over that the war has been won, the Iranian regime has been changed – and even more explicitly, that if the US left now, it would take Iran 20 years to rebuild. Loading There was also a Reuters report two weeks ago that said US intelligence agencies were analysing the likely consequences of Trump simply declaring mission accomplished and drawing down troops. That might be the least worst option. The US could credibly say it inflicted a lot of damage and set back Iran’s nuclear ambitions again, while reserving the right to revisit the matter down the track.





While always keeping on the table further military action, Trump has been reluctant to go down that path. Not only is the war unpopular with Americans, but he would have to answer the question of what fresh strikes would achieve that was not achieved in the first 37 days of intense bombing. Related Article China relations The five ‘Bs’ and three ‘Ts’ at the heart of the Trump-Xi meeting By delaying its inevitably unsatisfactory response, which was initially going to come last week, Iran has also forced Trump into an awkward position in the days before his important trip to China. Restarting strikes could jeopardise the visit. But arriving in Beijing without a credible path forward and asking Chinese President Xi Jinping for help in corralling the Iranians looks weak. A senior US official said Trump would probably pressure Xi to curb the sale of dual-use components and potential weapons to Iran, as he had done in the past.



“I expect that conversation to continue,” the official said on a phone call with reporters on Sunday (US time). “You’ve seen some actions, meaning sanctions, coming out from the US side in the last few days that I’m sure will be part of that conversation. “I would expect the president to apply pressure … he has done so before.” View post on X Vali Nasr, an Iran expert and professor of international affairs at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland, noted that applying such pressure on Xi would not be easy. The Chinese would seek to extract something in return for their help, Nasr said on X – and they could still say no. The Beijing summit would then be “another casualty of the war”. World.title: State clears 70 per cent of DNA backlog, returns to testing in July
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government State clears 70 per cent of DNA backlog, returns to testing in July Catherine Strohfeldt May 11, 2026 — 3:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A backlog of 600 samples linked to rape investigations in Queensland has been cleared by the state laboratory following the DNA bungle that botched testing of samples from thousands of major crimes. Attorney-general Deb Frecklington said the state had increased the number of scientists from 19 to 24 at the state lab, Forensic Science Queensland, and appointed two new members to its leadership board. She said the state had also cleared 70 per cent of samples from major crimes that had been awaiting testing since November – equating to more than 8200 samples. Forensic Science Queensland and former NSW police commissioner Mick Fuller. Catherine Strohfeldt “These aren’t just numbers, these are people who were waiting and left waiting,” Frecklington said.



Related Article Queensland government Qld’s ‘dirty lab’ leaves rape victims at risk of further assault: report The lab has been in a perpetual state of scandal since late 2021 and the centre of two landmark commissions of inquiry after former forensic biologist Dr Kirsty Wright blew the whistle on alleged testing failures in the 2013 murder investigation of Shandee Blackburn. FSQ is a statutory authority established to respond to the bungle in 2023 following revelations cracks in Queensland’s then automated DNA extraction method might have led to offenders escaping conviction from 2007 to 2016. However, a report released in June indicated that from early 2023, scientists had knowingly been testing samples in a “dirty lab”, meaning some results given to police and used to prosecute cases were unreliable. In late 2025, the state began outsourcing testing to United States forensics laboratory Bode Technology.





“The goal [of] mine is to restart the sexual assault testing in probably July this year, which means that we could be turning around results within five or 10 working days,” he said. The state had also retested results for about 20,000 previously analysed samples, from an initial 40,000 that fell within the scope of a historical review process. In June last year, the lab had tested 10,000 of the flagged samples. Fuller previously said he expected the state could clear about 1000 major crime samples and 175 forensic medical examination kits per month but reiterated on Monday clearing the backlog would take “an enormous amount of time”. “It’s just not about grabbing a vial and retesting – you really have to look at continuity of all aspects of it, but we are reducing it,” he said.



The two new FSQ leadership members include UK Metropolitan Police forensic scientist Saranjeet Khera and long-time Justice Department worker Kirsten Eades. Shadow Attorney-General Meaghan Scanlon said on Monday the backlog had begun to be reduced under the former Labor government. “Ultimately some of these issues have been over a long period of time over both sides of politics, and I think everyone wants to see justice delivered to victims of crime, and this really should be a bipartisan issue,” she told reporters outside Parliament House.
